topics.title: Scope, Significance and Definition of Construction Contracts
explain: AS 7 prescribes accounting for construction contracts in contractor financial statements.
A construction contract is specifically negotiated for constructing an asset or interrelated assets.
It applies to long-term projects spanning more than one accounting period.
It applies when there are two separate parties: the contractor and the contractee.
Self-constructed assets built for internal entity use fall under AS 10, not AS 7.
AS 7 also covers related service contracts (e.g., architects) and demolition or restoration contracts.

flow.title: Determining if AS 7 Applies
steps: Contract negotiated for construction/restoration
Two separate parties exist (Contractor & Customer)
Spans across accounting periods
Apply AS 7 for revenue & cost recognition

topics.example: A company signing a 3-year contract with the state government to construct a flyover.
remember: AS 7 applies to contractors, not customers.
Internal asset construction is covered by AS 10 (PPE).
mistakes: Applying AS 7 to a machine built by a company's own engineering division for its own factory.

quiz.q: Which of the following falls under the scope of AS 7?
o: An entity constructing a machine for its own production division
A contractor constructing a bridge for a municipality
Sale of standard manufactured goods from inventory
Purchasing ready-made office furniture
quiz.why: AS 7 covers construction contracts negotiated with external customers, not self-constructed assets.

quiz.q: Besides asset construction, AS 7 also explicitly includes:
o: General audit services
Contracts for destruction or restoration of assets
Employee salary negotiation contracts
Supply of raw inventory goods
quiz.why: AS 7 explicitly includes contracts for demolition, restoration of assets, and directly related project management/architect services.

topics.title: Combining and Segmenting Construction Contracts
explain: A single contract covering multiple assets must be segmented into separate contracts if separate proposals were submitted, separate negotiations occurred, and costs/revenues are identifiable.
A group of contracts with single or multiple customers must be combined as one single contract if negotiated as a single package with an overall profit margin and executed concurrently.
An additional asset requested by a customer is treated as a separate contract if it differs significantly in design/function or its price is negotiated separately.

flow.title: Contract Combination and Segmentation Test
steps: Inspect contract structure & assets covered
Check if assets had separate proposals & negotiations
If yes, segment into separate contracts
If package deal with overall margin, combine contracts

topics.example: Building 2 residential blocks on one site under a single package price with an overall margin is treated as a single combined contract.
remember: Segmenting requires separate proposals, separate negotiations, and identifiable revenues/costs.
Combining requires a single negotiated package, interrelated project, and overall profit margin.
mistakes: Treating an additional floor constructed under a freshly negotiated fee as part of the original contract instead of a separate contract.

quiz.q: When should a single contract covering multiple assets be segmented under AS 7?
o: When all assets are constructed in different countries
When separate proposals were submitted and separate negotiations took place for each asset
Only if the customer requests it after project completion
Never, a single document must always be treated as one contract
quiz.why: Segmenting is required when separate proposals, separate negotiations, and identifiable costs/revenues exist for each asset.

quiz.q: An additional asset added to a contract is treated as a separate construction contract if:
o: It is built in the same month as the main asset
Its price is negotiated without regard to the original contract price
The customer pays in cash instead of bank transfer
It costs less than 5% of the original contract
quiz.why: Additional assets are treated as separate contracts if they differ significantly in design/function or are negotiated independently of the original price.

topics.title: Types of Construction Contracts
explain: Fixed Price Contract: The contractor agrees to a fixed contract sum or fixed rate per unit of output.
Fixed price contracts may contain cost escalation clauses allowing recovery of wage/material cost increases.
Cost-Plus Contract: The contractor is reimbursed for allowable costs plus an agreed percentage or fixed fee.
Cost-plus contracts are used when there is high uncertainty regarding total costs or project duration.

flow.title: Classifying Contract Type
steps: Identify price terms in contract
Is total sum or rate per unit fixed upfront?
If fixed (with or without escalation clauses) -> Fixed Price Contract
If costs reimbursed + profit margin -> Cost-Plus Contract

topics.example: A tender to build an office building for a fixed price of ₹50 Crore with a clause to recover material price hikes above 10% is a Fixed Price Contract.
remember: Cost-escalation clauses do not change a fixed price contract into a cost-plus contract.
mistakes: Thinking a fixed price contract cannot have any price adjustments for cost escalations.

quiz.q: What defines a Cost-Plus Contract under AS 7?
o: The contractor pays a fixed fine if delayed
The contractor is reimbursed defined costs plus a percentage or fixed fee
The price is fixed permanently with no adjustments allowed
The customer pays only after 10 years
quiz.why: Cost-plus contracts reimburse defined allowable costs plus an agreed profit margin or fixed fee.

quiz.q: Including a cost-escalation clause in a contract makes it:
o: A Cost-Plus Contract
A Fixed Price Contract with escalation terms
An invalid contract under AS 7
A service contract
quiz.why: Cost escalation clauses protect against cost spikes but still leave the underlying agreement as a fixed price contract.

topics.title: Contract Revenue and Contract Costs
explain: Contract Revenue includes initial agreed amount, variations, claims, and incentive payments (if probable and measurable), minus penalties.
Claims and incentives are included in revenue only when approval is probable and the amount can be measured reliably.

Contract Costs include direct costs (site labor, materials, depreciation of used equipment), indirect allocable costs (insurance, allocable borrowing costs under AS 16), and specifically chargeable customer costs.
Direct costs are reduced by incidental income, such as sale of surplus materials.
Excluded Costs: General admin costs (unless reimbursable), selling costs, R&D costs, and idle plant depreciation.

flow.title: Determining Total Contract Revenue & Costs
steps: Start with initial agreed revenue
Add probable claims, incentives, variations & subtract penalties
Sum direct costs + allocable indirect overheads + chargeable costs
Deduct incidental income & exclude selling/admin costs

topics.example: Selling unused site steel for ₹2 Lakhs reduces direct site material costs rather than being treated as main revenue.
remember: Incentive payments are recognized only when performance standards are likely to be met or exceeded.
General selling and administrative costs are excluded from contract costs.
mistakes: Including general selling or showroom expenses in contract costs.

quiz.q: Which of the following is EXCLUDED from contract costs under AS 7?
o: Site labor supervision costs
Depreciation of equipment used on site
Selling and marketing costs
Costs of hiring site machinery
quiz.why: Selling costs cannot be attributed to specific contract activity and must be excluded.

quiz.q: How is incidental income from selling surplus site materials treated under AS 7?
o: Recognized as main contract revenue
Deducted directly from direct contract costs
Ignored completely in financial accounting
Credited to capital reserve
quiz.why: Incidental income reduces direct contract costs.

topics.title: Percentage Completion Method & Stage of Completion
explain: Contract revenue and expenses are recognized in proportion to the stage of completion at the reporting date.
This method applies accrual and matching concepts to long-term construction contracts.
Conditions for Fixed Price: Revenue measurable, economic benefits probable, costs to complete & stage measurable, costs attributable clearly identifiable.
Conditions for Cost-Plus: Benefits probable, attributable costs clearly identifiable.
Ways to compute Stage of Completion: (1) Cost proportion method (Actual costs to date / Total estimated costs), (2) Survey of work performed, (3) Physical proportion of work completed.

flow.title: Percentage Completion Revenue Calculation
steps: Determine actual costs incurred to date
Calculate stage of completion % = (Cost to date / Total estimated cost) * 100
Cumulative Revenue = Total Contract Revenue * Stage %
Current Year Revenue = Cumulative Revenue - Revenue recognized in prior years

topics.example: If total agreed contract value is ₹100 Lakhs, and actual cost incurred to date is ₹30 Lakhs out of ₹60 Lakhs total expected cost, stage of completion is 50%, so cumulative revenue recognized is ₹50 Lakhs.
remember: Stage of Completion % = Cost incurred to date / Total estimated cost (Actual cost incurred + Estimated future cost).
mistakes: Using progress payments or customer advances as the percentage of work completed.

quiz.q: Under the cost proportion method, stage of completion is calculated as:
o: Advances received / Total contract price
Actual costs incurred to date / Total estimated contract costs
Progress payments billed / Total contract price
Work certified by customer / Customer payments received
quiz.why: Stage of completion = Actual costs incurred to date divided by total estimated contract costs.

quiz.q: Progress payments and customer advances received reflect:
o: The exact percentage of work performed
Not necessarily the stage of completion or actual work performed
The absolute contract profit
Total recoverable costs under all circumstances
quiz.why: Advances and progress payments are cash flows and do not necessarily represent the actual stage of completion.

topics.title: Expected Losses, Uncertain Outcomes & Uncollectable Revenue
explain: Rule of Prudence: Whenever total contract costs exceed total contract revenue, the entire expected loss must be recognized as an expense immediately.
If outcome of a contract CANNOT be estimated reliably: Revenue is recognized only to the extent of incurred contract costs that are probable of recovery.
When outcome cannot be estimated reliably, contract costs are expensed in the period incurred (resulting in zero profit).
If uncertainty arises about collecting an amount already included in revenue, the uncollectable amount is expensed separately, not deducted from original revenue.

flow.title: Accounting for Expected Loss
steps: Estimate Total Contract Cost (Costs to date + Future costs)
Compare with Total Contract Revenue
If Total Cost > Total Revenue -> Foreseeable Loss exists
Recognize full foreseeable loss in Profit & Loss immediately

topics.example: If total revenue is ₹85 Lakhs and total estimated cost spikes to ₹97 Lakhs, the full expected loss of ₹12 Lakhs must be provided in P&L immediately.
remember: Expected losses are recognized in full immediately regardless of the stage of completion.
Uncollectable revenue is charged as an expense, not adjusted against revenue.
mistakes: Deferring expected contract losses over remaining years of the contract instead of recognizing them immediately.

quiz.q: When total contract costs are expected to exceed total contract revenue, how should the expected loss be treated under AS 7?
o: Recognized as an expense immediately in full
Amortized equally over the remaining contract period
Deducted from customer advance balance
Ignored until the contract is fully finished
quiz.why: AS 7 requires immediate recognition of the total foreseeable loss in full under the prudence concept.

quiz.q: If the outcome of a construction contract cannot be estimated reliably, revenue should be recognized:
o: Equal to total contract price upfront
Only to the extent of contract costs incurred whose recovery is probable
At a mandatory standard rate of 10% profit margin
Zero revenue until final completion year
quiz.why: When outcome cannot be estimated reliably, revenue is recognized only up to recoverable costs incurred.

topics.title: Disclosures and Financial Statement Presentation
explain: General Disclosures: Revenue recognized in the period, methods used to determine contract revenue, and methods used for stage of completion.
Contracts in Progress Disclosures: Aggregate costs incurred + recognized profits (less recognized losses), advances received, and retention amounts.
Retentions: Billed amounts held back by customer until specific conditions or defect rectifications are satisfied.
Progress Billings: Amounts billed for work performed, whether paid by customer or not.
Balance Sheet Presentation: Compute Net Amount = (Costs incurred + Recognized profits - Recognized losses) - Progress billings.
If Net Amount is positive -> Present as 'Gross amount due from customers' (Asset).
If Net Amount is negative -> Present as 'Gross amount due to customers' (Liability).

flow.title: Calculating Due From / To Customers
steps: Take Costs Incurred to Date
Add Recognized Profits & Subtract Recognized Losses
Subtract Progress Billings Billed to Customer
Positive result = Asset (Due from Customers); Negative result = Liability (Due to Customers)

topics.example: If costs + net profit = ₹505 Lakhs, and progress billings = ₹540 Lakhs, net balance is -₹35 Lakhs, presented as a liability (Gross amount due to customers).
remember: Progress billings are deducted from (Costs + Net Profits/Losses) to determine asset or liability status.
Retentions are billed amounts not yet paid by contractee.
mistakes: Subtracting advances received instead of progress billings when computing Gross Amount Due From/To Customers.

quiz.q: How is 'Gross Amount Due From Customers' calculated for balance sheet presentation under AS 7?
o: Costs incurred + Progress billings - Retention
(Costs incurred + Recognized profits - Recognized losses) - Progress billings
Total contract price - Cash received
Customer advances + Retentions - Bank balance
quiz.why: Net amount due = (Costs incurred + Recognized profits - Recognized losses) - Progress billings.

quiz.q: Amounts billed for work performed on a contract but held back by customer until defect rectification are called:
o: Advances
Retentions
Foreseeable losses
Cost escalation claims
quiz.why: Retentions are progress billings not paid until specified contract conditions or defect rectifications are satisfied.
